content: The Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) is a nonprofit advocacy organization headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA. Its membership includes both professional scientists and private citizens. The UCS Board of Directors is chaired by Kurt Gottfried, a former senior staff member at CERN. The organization is also a member of the Sustainable Energy Coalition. The UCS advocates for stricter Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards and aims to reduce smog pollution caused by construction equipment and diesel trucks. It supports state-level legislation to lower greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles, modeled after California's regulations. The organization calls for significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions across the United States and promotes both national and international efforts to address climate change. It has published multiple reports detailing the regional impacts of climate change within the United States. The UCS endorses a national renewable electricity standard, which would mandate that utilities generate a specific percentage of their energy from renewable sources such as wind, solar, and geothermal. While the organization acknowledges that nuclear power has the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, it insists that nuclear energy must become significantly safer and more cost-effective before it can be considered a viable solution to global warming. The UCS monitors instances of political interference in scientific research and supports protections for whistleblowers and the free speech rights of federal scientists. Its scientific integrity program has conducted surveys of federal scientists across various agencies and has issued a statement, signed by over 11,000 scientists, condemning political interference in science. The organization opposes the overuse of antibiotics in livestock, citing concerns about the development of antibiotic resistance in humans who consume treated animals. It also opposes the cloning of animals for food and certain forms of genetic engineering. The UCS is against the deployment of space weapons and advocates for an international treaty to regulate military activities in space. Additionally, the group works to reduce the global stockpile of nuclear weapons and opposes the Reliable Replacement Warhead program. It has also criticized the technical feasibility of constructing a missile defense shield. The UCS was founded in 1969 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) by faculty and students. One of its co-founders, physicist and Nobel laureate Dr. Henry Kendall, served as the chairman of the board for many years. In 1977, the UCS sponsored a Scientists' Declaration on the Nuclear Arms Race, which called for an end to nuclear weapons testing and deployment in both the United States and the Soviet Union. In response to the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), the UCS launched a petition titled An Appeal to Ban Space Weapons. In 1992, Dr. Kendall presided over the UCS's Warning to Humanity, a document signed by 1,700 scientists, including a majority of Nobel laureates in the sciences, which called for fundamental changes to address various security and environmental challenges. Between 2000 and 2002, the UCS was the fourth-largest recipient of foundation grants for climate studies, with a quarter of its $24 million grant income allocated to this purpose. In 1997, the UCS circulated a petition titled A Call to Action, urging the ratification of the Kyoto Protocol. This petition was signed by 110 Nobel laureates, including 104 Nobel Prize-winning scientists. In February 2004, the UCS gained media attention for its report Scientific Integrity in Policymaking, which accused the administration of U.S. President George W. Bush of politicizing science. Allegations included altering Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports on global warming and selecting members of scientific advisory panels based on business interests rather than scientific expertise. In July 2004, the UCS released an addendum to the report, further criticizing the Bush administration for allegedly altering reports on strip mining in West Virginia and rejecting well-qualified nominees for government positions, such as Nobel laureate Torsten Wiesel, due to political differences. On April 2, 2004, Dr. John Marburger, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, issued a statement dismissing the UCS report as biased and claiming that its descriptions of incidents were false, wrong, or distorted. The UCS rebutted these claims, stating that Marburger's criticisms were unfounded. The organization later noted that the Bush administration had remained largely silent on the issue since that time. On October 15, 2005, the UCS announced the creation of a new Scientific Integrity Program to address politically motivated interference in science and to advocate for scientific integrity. On October 30, 2006, the UCS issued a press release accusing senior officials at the U.S. Department of the Interior, including Deputy Assistant Secretary for Fish and Wildlife and Parks Julie MacDonald, of systematically tampering with scientific data to undermine the Endangered Species Act and the protection of endangered species. On December 11, 2006, the UCS released a statement signed by 10,600 leading scientists, including Nobel laureates, calling for the restoration of scientific integrity in federal policymaking. On May 23, 2007, the UCS, in collaboration with MIT, issued a press release criticizing the U.S. missile defense system. The organization argued that any test of the system that fails to demonstrate the ability to distinguish between real warheads and decoys is irrelevant and contrived. The UCS called for an end to taxpayer funding for the program until it could prove its effectiveness against real-world threats. On June 21, 2007, the UCS released a report documenting the political manipulation of scientific data to influence updated U.S. ozone regulations. Francesca Grifo, director of the UCS's Scientific Integrity Program, stated, The law says use the science, the science says lower the standard to safe levels. She criticized the EPA for disregarding its own scientists' analyses, thereby endangering the health of millions of Americans. The UCS has faced criticism from free-market and pro-capitalism advocacy groups for its positions on environmental and regulatory issues. Fred Singer, a professor at the University of Virginia and founder of the Science & Environmental Policy Project, has stated that the UCS has zero credibility as a scientific organization. The UCS, in turn, has referred to Singer as a climate contrarian. Brent Bozell, head of the Media Research Center, has described the UCS as a left-wing activist organization with a left-wing activist political agenda, accusing it of falsely presenting itself as an objective and apolitical entity.
